subject: Chemistry
title: Neon: The Light of the City
description: A quick, practical guide to Neon: The Light of the City.

hook.text: We call all glowing signs 'neon lights,' but real neon glows only one color: reddish-orange.

buildup.text: William Ramsay and Morris Travers discovered neon in 1898 by chilling air and separating its gases.

discovery.text: When they ran electricity through it, neon glowed a brilliant crimson red. Travers called it 'a blaze of crimson.'

twist.text: Georges Claude made the first neon sign in 1910. By the 1930s, neon lit up Times Square and Las Vegas.

climax.text: Other gas colors—blue for mercury, green for argon—get called 'neon' too, but only neon makes red.

punchline.text: Only reddish-orange is real neon. Everything else is an imposter.

quiz.question: What color does pure neon gas produce when electrified?

details.summary: Neon was discovered by William Ramsay and Morris Travers in 1898 by fractional distillation of liquid air. When they passed electricity through the isolated gas, it emitted a brilliant reddish-orange glow that Travers described as blinding crimson..
details.whyItMatters: Neon transformed urban landscapes worldwide through neon signage, becoming an iconic symbol of modern cities. Neon lighting technology also advanced understanding of atomic spectral emission.
takeaways: Neon was isolated from liquid air using fractional distillation in 1898
Its distinctive reddish-orange glow comes from electron energy transitions
Georges Claude created the first neon signs in Paris around 1910

faq.question: Why does neon glow such a distinctive reddish-orange color?
faq.answer: When electricity excites neon atoms, their electrons jump to higher energy levels. As electrons fall back, they release energy as light at specific wavelengths..

faq.question: Are most neon signs actually filled with neon gas?
faq.answer: No. Only red and orange signs use actual neon gas. Other colors use different gases: blue comes from argon with mercury vapor, green from argon with mercury plus phosphor coating, and white from various gas-phosphor combinations..
